Rank-ordered (exploded) logit regression

Source: R/rologit.R
rologit.Rd

Fits the rank-ordered logit (Beggs, Cardell and Hausman 1981, who call it the ordered logit), also called the exploded logit after Chapman and Staelin's (1982) "explosion" of a ranking into independent choices (Allison and Christakis 1994): the model for data in which each case ranks some or all of its available alternatives, such as survey rankings of parties or candidates, or the ballots of a ranked-choice election. With the utilities of mnl(), a ranking is a sequence of multinomial-logit choices: the first-ranked alternative is chosen from the whole choice set, the second from those left, and so on. Rankings carry more information than first choices, so the same coefficients are estimated more precisely than from the first choices alone.

Usage

rologit(
  formula,
  data,
  id,
  alt,
  ref = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  depth = NULL,
  se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"),
  cluster = NULL,
  nboot = 200L,
  cores = 1L,
  start = NULL,
  maxit = 1000L,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  firth = FALSE,
  prior = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

rank ~ w | x (see Details); rank ~ w without case-specific covariates.

data

A data frame.

id, alt

Names of the case and alternative columns of data.

ref

The base alternative: a level of the alternative column alt (default: its first level), whose constant and case-specific coefficients are zero.

weights

Optional frequency weights: a column name in data or a numeric vector with one entry per row (constant within a case in the long layout).

offset

Optional offset on the utility scale: a column name of data or a vector with one entry per row.

depth

Optional: use only the first depth positions of every ranking; alternatives ranked below become unranked (a tie group that starts within the first depth positions is kept whole). depth = 1 is the multinomial logit of the first choices.

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (inverse observed information, default), "opg", "robust", "cluster" (needs cluster), "bootstrap" (nonparametric over cases, or over clusters when cluster is given, with nboot refits), or "none".

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows, constant within a case); supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

nboot

Number of bootstrap refits for se = "bootstrap" (default 200).

cores

Number of parallel workers for the bootstrap (a PSOCK cluster; default 1). set.seed() before the call makes the resamples reproducible; serial and parallel runs use different random streams.

start

Optional starting values: the full parameter vector in the order of coef() (object$theta of an earlier fit); rarely needed, since the log-likelihood is globally concave.

maxit, reltol

Controls for the BFGS stage passed to stats::optim() (the plain mnl() is solved by damped Newton steps first, with BFGS as the fallback); the Newton polish that follows runs up to 25 further iterations with the analytic Hessian of the logit family or central differences of the analytic gradient otherwise.

firth

If TRUE, Firth's penalized likelihood (see Details); default FALSE, maximum likelihood. Weights are read as frequency weights and must total more than 2.

prior

Optional: priors for the coefficients, made by coef_prior(); the fit is the posterior mode, a penalized fit like firth = TRUE. Not with firth = TRUE.

Value

An object of class c("rologit", "choicemodel"), with the components of an mnl() fit; design$str$rank holds the rankings used (dense ranks by case, 0 for unranked or unavailable alternatives).

Details

Case \(i\) ranks the alternatives \(r_{i1}, r_{i2}, \dots\) of its choice set \(A_i\); with \(R_{il}\) the alternatives not ranked before position \(l\), $$\log L_i = \sum_l \Big[ V_{i r_{il}} - \log \sum_{m \in R_{il}} e^{V_{im}} \Big],$$ with \(V_{ij}\) as in mnl(). The log-likelihood is globally concave. Partial rankings (the first few positions ranked, the rest left unranked) are handled exactly: the unranked alternatives are tied below every ranked one and contribute only through the denominators. Ties among ranked alternatives are handled by the exact likelihood of Allison and Christakis (1994, eq. 8): the tied alternatives are taken to have an unknown strict order, and the likelihood sums over every order (at most 7 tied alternatives above others; Breslow's approximation, the default of proportional-hazards software, attenuates the estimates and is not used).

The model assumes that the relative preference for two alternatives does not depend on which alternatives have already been ranked: independence of irrelevant alternatives at every stage. Respondents may rank the first positions more carefully than the later ones: Chapman and Staelin (1982) and Hausman and Ruud (1987) argue, and find in their applications, that later ranks can be noisier, Hausman and Ruud adding that the pattern depends on the survey. rank_test() tests whether the coefficients differ between early and late stages, and depth limits the fit to the first positions (Chapman and Staelin's explosion depth, Hausman and Ruud's top-P estimator; with only the first position, the model is the multinomial logit of the first choices).

The data are in the long layout: one row per case and available alternative, with id and alt naming the case and alternative columns, as in mnl(). The response is the rank: smaller numbers are preferred, equal numbers are ties (the numbers need only be in the right order), and 0 marks an alternative left unranked.

  • An unranked alternative is in the choice set, below every ranked one: it enters the denominators of every stage (the respondent saw it and did not rank it).

  • An alternative without a row for the case is unavailable and enters none. Drop a row only where the alternative was not on offer.

  • Without a penalty, ties are exact up to 7 alternatives tied above others. A larger tie group above other alternatives is refused, and a tie at the bottom, below no other alternative, is unlimited.

The formula is rank ~ w | x: alternative-specific covariates with generic coefficients, then case-specific covariates with alternative-specific coefficients. Cases in which no alternative is ranked above another carry no information and are dropped with a message. Weights, offsets, clusters, and standard errors are as in mnl(); a case (one ranking) is the observation. Unit fixed effects are not available.

Fitted values, predict(), first_difference(), and rrr() describe first choices: the multinomial-logit probabilities over the choice set. predict(type = "ranking") gives the probability of each observed ranking. y holds each case's first choice (with a tie at the top, the first of the tied alternatives in level order), which is what classification(), the count measures of fit_stats(), and residuals() use; the log-likelihood measures of fit_stats() are those of the rankings, against the rank-ordered logit with alternative-specific constants only. simulate() draws rankings. The tests of the independence of irrelevant alternatives and the goodness-of-fit test apply to single-choice fits and refuse a rank-ordered one; lr_test() and vuong() compare two rank-ordered fits of the same rankings.

Separation occurs in rankings as in single choices: when a combination of the covariates ranks every observed choice first among the alternatives still unranked at its position, the maximum-likelihood estimates run off (the monotone likelihood of the Cox model, of which this is the version stratified by case; Bryson and Johnson 1981). Ranking fewer positions (depth, or partial rankings) leaves fewer such constraints and makes it more likely. The maximum-likelihood fit decides it exactly (the linear program of separation(), ties as groups) and names the diverging coefficients in a warning; an alternative never ranked above another available one is the simplest case (its constant runs to minus infinity). firth = TRUE penalizes the log-likelihood by half the log-determinant of its information, the sum over the stages of each ranking of the information of the stage's choice given the alternatives left: Heinze and Schemper's (2001) penalty for the Cox model, with one stratum per case. A tie group of \(d\) alternatives enters with the information of the exact tie probability (the probability that the tied set is the top \(d\) of the alternatives left), the expected information of that outcome over the possible sets, which reduces to the conditional-logit information of an untied position. The estimates are finite under separation; the rest is as for mnl() (section "Penalized (Firth) estimation"): the log-likelihood at the penalized estimates, standard errors from the inverse information, the separated coefficients in separation, the run from a second start, profile intervals from confint(), and penalized likelihood-ratio tests from term_test(), lr_test() and rank_test(). Under the penalty or a prior a tie group is refused when more than 62 alternatives remain at its positions, when it has more than \(10^5\) subsets of them to enumerate, or (Firth's penalty) when the second derivatives of its subsets would need more than 200 MB; without a penalty only ties of more than 7 alternatives ranked above others are refused.

References

Allison, P.D. and Christakis, N.A. (1994). Logit models for sets of ranked items. Sociological Methodology, 24, 199-228. doi:10.2307/270983

Beggs, S., Cardell, S. and Hausman, J. (1981). Assessing the potential demand for electric cars. Journal of Econometrics, 17, 1-19. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(81)90056-7

Bryson, M.C. and Johnson, M.E. (1981). The incidence of monotone likelihood in the Cox model. Technometrics, 23, 381-383. doi:10.1080/00401706.1981.10487683

Chapman, R.G. and Staelin, R. (1982). Exploiting rank ordered choice set data within the stochastic utility model. Journal of Marketing Research, 19, 288-301. doi:10.1177/002224378201900302

Hausman, J.A. and Ruud, P.A. (1987). Specifying and testing econometric models for rank-ordered data. Journal of Econometrics, 34, 83-104. doi:10.1016/0304-4076(87)90068-6

Heinze, G. and Schemper, M. (2001). A solution to the problem of monotone likelihood in Cox regression. Biometrics, 57, 114-119. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00114.x

See also

rank_test(), rrologit(), mnl()

Other estimators: hev(), imnl(), mnl(), mnprobit(), nlogit(), remnl()

Examples

set.seed(4)
d <- rrologit(600, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5), d = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3)),
              gamma = 0.7, depth = 3)
head(d)
#>   id alt rank          w1         x1         x2
#> 1  1   a    2  0.03349124  0.2167549 -2.1532042
#> 2  1   b    0 -0.50828566  0.2167549 -2.1532042
#> 3  1   c    1 -0.28867304  0.2167549 -2.1532042
#> 4  1   d    3  0.85654205  0.2167549 -2.1532042
#> 5  2   a    3 -1.45849674 -0.5424926 -0.5727423
#> 6  2   b    1  1.65373350 -0.5424926 -0.5727423
m <- rologit(rank ~ w1 | x1 + x2, data = d, id = "id", alt = "alt")
summary(m)
#> Rank-ordered logit
